record.experiment_description:
OBJECTIVES:
Although some portions of the musculoskeletal system have been examined as part of other astronaut examinations (doctor’s physical, stress test, X-rays, et cetera) there has been no specific integrated examination for this largest system of the human body. Conversely, the musculoskeletal system plays a primary role in space operations and research. The state of muscles and the subject’s use of them determines, not only their condition and potential performance, but also condition of the cardiovascular and respiratory system on Earth and in space. Defects or limitations of this system can make it impossible for a subject to perform essential functions in operation and thus are disqualifying. A number of such limitations are specified in the physical requirements, but measurement of them requires equipment and techniques not usually available to the flight surgeon. Anthropometric measurements are urgently required by many man-machine designers in the space program. Anthropometric data have also become increasingly important as a research tool for investigation of effects of weightlessness of the body. Such information is particularly important for Shuttle, which is accepting an entirely new space-flight population.

APPROACH:
In 1978, approximately 207 astronaut candidates were examined during a NASA astronaut selection for the first Space Shuttle missions. Of this number, 80% were men and 20% were women. The crew positions to be assigned included male pilots, and both male and female mission specialists.

Basic physical examinations were conducted in addition to numerous specialty exams. The tests included a treadmill stress test and musculoskeletal examinations of each candidate. The treadmill test used the standard Balke-Ware protocol. The musculoskeletal exam consisted of a detailed history and physical examination, a large series of anthropometric measurements, and strength testing of major muscle groups by means of an isokinetic ergometer.

RESULTS:
The results of the examinations were immediately supplied to the medical examination board to use in the selection process. As expected from historical and general experience, the females were significantly weaker than the males, especially in the upper extremities. Also, as in general experience, there were one or two exceptionally strong females well outside the normal range in the entire group of females. This difference was most marked in the upper extremities when absolute comparisons were made. If strength relative to body weight in pilot candidates, male mission specialist candidates, and female mission specialist candidates were compared, the difference was less but marked. Since body fat was so different in males versus females (15 percent versus 25 percent in this case), the question was raised as to what happens if the female singly loses weight. This was indicated by calculating strength per lean body mass. In this case, back and leg differences in strength were much less, but arm and shoulder strength remained significantly different.

Some minor surprises were the differences in shoulder and back strength in pilots and mission specialists. Mission specialists were stronger in both areas even when they were normalized for body weight and lean body mass. As a matter of fact, the females had greater back strength on the basis of lean body mass than the pilots.

dataset_info.dataset_name: Regression Parameters on Body Weight (for selected individuals)
dataset_description: This is a printout of regression parameters for each anthropometric measurement collected on 35 astronaut candidates in 1977.  The printout is not dated.  For each parameter measured, regression parameters A and B, plus the standard error estimate are given.  No additional information is available.  Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

This file is a computer printout of eight parameters measured on 200+ astronaut candidates in 1977.  Males and females, both selected and non-selected candidates, are included in the printout.  The original software used to generate the spreadsheet appears to be FORTRAN.  The paper computer printout was scanned into PDF format for archiving purposes.  Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

This file is a computer printout of four wrist anthropometric measurements collected on astronaut candidates in 1977. No supporting information is available to describe the data.

Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

This spreadsheet is a summarization of the anthropometric measurements collected on astronaut candidates in 1977.  The results are broken down into two groupings: pilots and mission specialists.  The data for mission specialists are further broken down into male and female groups. For each parameter, the mean, standard deviation, range, and number of subjects examined is provided.  Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

This is a draft document describing the fundamental procedures for obtaining measurements on astronaut candidates in 1977 using the Automatic Video Goniometer (AVG).

Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

This is a draft document describing the fundamental procedures for obtaining anthropometric measurements on astronaut candidates in 1977.

Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

dataset_info.dataset_name: Percentile Scores for Anthropometric Measurements on Mission Specialist and Pilot Candidates
dataset_description: This is a printout of percentile scores for each anthropometric measurement collected on astronaut candidates in 1977.  The printout is not dated.  For each parameter measured, the percentile scores (5%-95%) were calculated for all subjects, pilots, male mission specialists, female mission specialists, all males (as a group), and all mission specialists (as a group).  A normal distribution was assumed for all measurements.  Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

This is a printout of basic statistics for each anthropometric measurement collected on astronaut candidates in 1977.  The printout is not dated.  For each parameter measured, the mean, standard deviation, maximum and minimum values were calculated for all subjects, pilots, male mission specialists, female mission specialists, all males (as a group), and all mission specialists (as a group).  Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.

dataset_info.dataset_name: Printout of Anthropometric Measurements Collected on Astronaut Candidates in 1977
dataset_description: This is a printout of all anthropometric measurements collected on the astronaut candidates in 1977.  The printout is dated 8/18/1980.  When compared to a similar (undated) printout for the same group of candidates, this printout appears to have in some cases more data points and in other cases fewer data points depending on the parameter being measured.  Source: Data from the William E. Thornton collection.
